Find out on the ground; keying a microphone at a dark mountain field and getting nothing is not the moment to discover the sequence is different.

q: What does a white and green rotating beacon tell you, and what are the hours here?
a: Alternating white and green identifies a lighted land airport, and at 1A3 the beacon operates from sunset to sunrise. A beacon on during daylight hours in Class B, C, D or E surface airspace is a sign that the ground visibility is below 3 statute miles or the ceiling is below 1,000 feet, but at an uncontrolled field like 1A3 with no weather reporting that cue does not exist, because the beacon is simply on a sunset to sunrise schedule.

q: Who do you talk to at 1A3, and how do you announce yourself?
a: Nobody; it is self announce on CTAF 122.9, with no tower and no UNICOM listed. I announce the airport name first and last, give position and intentions ten miles out, entering the pattern, on downwind, base and final, and clear of the runway. In mountain terrain I also overfly the field well above pattern altitude to look for traffic and for the wind indicator, and I keep listening on 122.9 well before I arrive, since other traffic may be on the same shared frequency at nearby fields.

q: How would you get an IFR clearance out of 1A3?
a: By telephone, which is exactly what the Chart Supplement says: clearance delivery is by telephone and approach and departure service is from Atlanta Center. I would call the clearance delivery number before engine start, get the clearance and a void time, and depart to meet it. The practical point is that there is no clearance delivery frequency on the ground at a valley field, so the plan has to be made on the ramp with the engine shut down, not with the propeller turning.

q: What is 133.1 at Copperhill, and what is 342.425?
a: Approach and departure service from Atlanta Air Route Traffic Control Center through the Mount Oglethorpe remote communications air to ground site: 133.1 is the very high frequency civil frequency and 342.425 is the paired ultra high frequency used by military aircraft. That is my contact for flight following, for an instrument clearance in the air and for an emergency. Coverage depends on altitude, so if I cannot raise Atlanta down in the valley, the answer is to climb.

q: Where do you find NOTAMs for this trip, and what types are there?
a: From the FAA NOTAM search website, from a standard briefing through Flight Service on 1 800 WX BRIEF, or through a flight planning application; AIM, Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) System, describes the system. The types are NOTAM D, which covers navigation aids, public airports, services and hazards; flight data center NOTAMs, which cover regulatory matters such as temporary flight restrictions and changes to instrument procedures; pointer NOTAMs; special activity airspace NOTAMs; and military NOTAMs.

q: Which NOTAM would hurt this trip the most?
a: One that closes the runway or the fuel at 1A3, or an unlit obstruction or an out of service PAPI at a field with terrain on the approach and no weather reporting. On a route like this I also check for temporary flight restrictions, for special activity airspace, and for GPS interference testing NOTAMs, because the approaches at 1A3 are RNAV GPS and my navigation backup matters more over the mountains. I read them for both airports and along the route, not just the destination.

q: How do you confirm fuel and field condition before you go?
a: Chart Supplement entry first for the published services, NOTAMs second for what has changed, and then a telephone call to the airport manager, whose number is in the Chart Supplement. At a 24 hour self service field with no attendant and no UNICOM, the phone call is the only way to learn that the pump is down, the runway is being seal coated or the deer fence is broken. The Chart Supplement tells me what is supposed to be there; the phone call tells me what is there today.

q: What services would you look for at airports along the route, and where?
a: Fuel, runway length and surface, lighting, a tower or a common traffic advisory frequency, and whether anybody is on the field; the sectional gives me the quick version and the Chart Supplement gives me the detail. On the chart, the airport data block carries the field elevation, the longest runway, the CTAF and the lighting and fuel symbols, and a star on the symbol means rotating beacon operation. I write two or three such fields on the navigation log as my planned outs.

q: What do power lines, railroad tracks and a racetrack look like on a sectional?
a: Power transmission lines are drawn as a line with small towers along it, railroads as a line with cross ticks, and the various cultural features have their own symbols explained in the chart legend. Read the legend panel on the chart rather than guessing, because the symbols for a dual track railroad, an abandoned railroad, a power line and a pipeline are easy to confuse. Linear features like these make excellent checkpoints in the low country out of Walterboro.

q: Halfway along, Copperhill is going down. How do you pick a diversion field?
a: Fuel, weather, runway and terrain, in that order, and I picked the candidates before I took off. I want a field I can reach with reserve intact, that has reported weather I can actually see, with a runway long enough for the Warrior and terrain I can get into and out of. On this route that usually means a larger field back toward lower ground rather than another small strip deeper in the mountains. I write two or three candidate fields with frequencies on the navigation log.

q: Show me how you divert in the air with no GPS.
a: Fly the airplane, then turn toward the new field before doing anything else. Pick the field off the chart, turn to an approximate heading estimated from the chart, note the time and the fuel, then measure the distance and the course with a plotter or with the finger and the chart scale, compute groundspeed and time from the last known groundspeed, and refine the heading. Then tell ATC, get weather, and brief the arrival. The order matters: heading first, arithmetic second.

q: How do you estimate heading, time and fuel to a diversion field quickly?
a: Use round numbers. Measure the course against a line of longitude or with a plotter, apply the same wind correction angle you already know works for that general direction, and estimate the distance by eye against the chart scale or the latitude ticks, where one minute of latitude is one nautical mile. At 105 knots I cover 1.75 nautical miles per minute, so divide the distance by 1.75 for minutes, and multiply hours by 8.4 gallons for fuel. Refine once the airplane is pointed the right way.

q: What do you tell ATC when you divert?
a: Who I am, where I am, what I am doing and what I want. On this route that is Atlanta Center on 133.1: call sign, position, altitude, that I am diverting from 1A3 to the new field, and a request for any weather they have and for flight following to it. If I cannot reach them down low I climb, and if the diversion is because of weather closing in, I say so, because that changes the service they will try to give me.

q: What is your best glide speed, and is the number in your handbook the right one?
a: The best glide speed has to come from Piper Report VB-880 for serial 28-8116257, not from the 73 knots printed in the VB-1180 revision. That 73 knot figure and the glide chart it comes from are computed at 2,440 pounds, a weight this airplane cannot reach. Best glide speed decreases with weight, so at 2,277 pounds the correct speed is lower. I read the right book, and in the airplane I fly the speed on the placard and in the emergency checklist for this serial.

q: Engine failure over the ridges. Where do you go?
a: Downhill and downwind toward the valley floor, toward the largest clear area within glide, while I fly best glide and run the restart flow. Over forested ridges the realistic options are a river bank, a field in the valley bottom, a road, a clearcut or a lake shore. I turn toward lower ground immediately rather than spending altitude looking, because altitude over a ridge converts into reach only in the downhill direction, and the valley is where any flat ground will be.

q: How does rising terrain affect your glide footprint?
a: It cuts it, and it cuts it asymmetrically. The glide range is a ratio of height above the ground, not height above sea level, so flying toward terrain that rises 1,000 feet eats 1,000 feet of glide before I even start. Downhill the footprint stretches; uphill it collapses. That is the practical argument for crossing ridges high and at an angle, and for never routing along a valley at an altitude from which only the valley floor ahead is reachable.

q: What are your off-airport landing options over unbroken forest?
a: Plan for a controlled arrival into the tops rather than a landing, flown at minimum controllable airspeed, wings level, full flaps, fuel and ignition off, doors unlatched and harnesses tight. The aim is to use the canopy to dissipate energy and to protect the cabin. I look for a clearcut, a road, a river or a power line cut first; all of them beat trees. The passenger briefing before departure covers the harness, the doors and the fire extinguisher for exactly this reason.

q: Lost over the mountains with no GPS. Walk me through it.
a: The five Cs: climb, communicate, confess, comply and conserve. Climb for terrain clearance, radio range and radar coverage; communicate with Atlanta Center on 133.1 or Flight Service, or 121.5 if nothing else answers; confess that I am uncertain of my position; comply with the instructions I am given; and conserve fuel by setting an economical power setting and by not wandering. Before any of that, note the time and the heading so the dead reckoning position is not lost too.

q: Without talking to anyone, how would you fix your position using a VOR?
a: Tune and identify a VOR, center the needle with a FROM indication, and that radial is a line of position; where it crosses a road, a river or a ridge I can see on the chart is my position. A second VOR crossed with the first gives a fix without needing ground reference. The trap is the ambiguity between TO and FROM: a centered needle with TO gives the reciprocal radial, and plotting that outbound from the station puts you on exactly the wrong side of it.

q: How does terrain affect your radio and radar coverage on this route?
a: Both are line of sight, so a ridge between me and the antenna blocks them regardless of how close I am. Low in a valley at Copperhill I may not reach Atlanta Center at all, and radar coverage will be poor or absent. The remedy is altitude: climb before transmitting, and expect to lose both during the descent into 1A3. That is one more reason to tell Center my intentions before I start down rather than after I have lost them.

q: Who do you call in an emergency on this route, and on what frequency?
a: Atlanta Center on 133.1 if I am already in contact or can reach them, otherwise 121.5, the emergency frequency. I squawk 7700 on the transponder, which gets attention even where radio coverage is poor, and I use the word mayday for a distress situation or pan pan for urgency. On the Walterboro end I would use whatever approach control or center frequency I had been working, and near 1A3 I would also broadcast my intentions on CTAF 122.9 so that local traffic knows.

q: Would you fly into the valley at Copperhill at dusk with a lowering ceiling?
a: No, and I would make that decision long before I was over the valley. A one runway field at 1,789 feet with ridges on the approach and along the east side of the runway, a right hand pattern, no weather reporting, nonstandard pilot activated low intensity lighting and wildlife on the runway is a field to arrive at in good light and good weather. A lowering ceiling at dusk in mountain terrain removes every option at once, which is the definition of a trap.

q: What is your plan if you simply cannot get into 1A3?
a: Divert to the alternate I chose on the ground, with the fuel I planned for that purpose, and tell the customer. I pick an alternate that reports weather, has fuel and has a runway and terrain I can manage, and I set a decision point on the navigation log, defined by both position and fuel, at which I commit to 1A3 or turn. Deciding in advance is what keeps the decision from being made by the weather, the fuel gauge or the customer.

q: What do you brief your passenger before this flight?
a: Seat belts and harnesses, how the doors and the emergency exit work, the fire extinguisher location, no smoking, the sterile cockpit periods and when I need quiet, what to do if I become incapacitated, and that I would like to be told about any traffic, bird or hazard they see. On this trip I would add the route, the expected two hours and a bit, the turbulence likely near the mountains, and the plain statement that we may divert and that the decision is mine.

q: You clip a runway light landing at 1A3. Is that reportable, and where do you look?
a: Look in 49 CFR Part 830, Notification and Reporting of Aircraft Accidents or Incidents and Overdue Aircraft, and Preservation of Aircraft Wreckage, Mail, Cargo, and Records, not in the Federal Aviation Regulations. Part 830 defines an accident by death or serious injury or substantial damage to the aircraft, and 830.5 lists the serious incidents that require immediate notification of the National Transportation Safety Board. Damage to a runway light alone is not on that list; damage to the airplane may change the answer.
